title: Speranza's Son and Prisoner C.3.3.: Wilde from Merrion Square to Pere Lachaise
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Westland Row, Dublin: the second son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde). Coordinate corrected: the research pool gave 53.3453, -6.2513, which lands about 290 metres north of the street at the Pearse Street end. Wikipedia's Westland Row point is 53.34278, -6.25, and Wikipedia's own 'Oscar Wilde Centre' figure of 53.34444, -6.25833 is a loose Trinity campus point rather than the house. The value used here is No. 21 itself, approximate to within a few doors.
stops.campa: In a narrow house on Westland Row, a few hundred yards from the college gates, a second son is born to William Wilde, eye and ear surgeon to half of Dublin, and to Jane Elgee, who has been writing insurrectionary verse for The Nation over the name Speranza since before her marriage. The father will be knighted for compiling a medical census of Ireland. The mother has had herself painted as a nation in mourning, and keeps the portrait. They give the child four names, three of them out of Irish legend and the fourth out of the family: Oscar Fingal O'Fflahertie Wills.
suggested_refs: 21 Westland Row, Dublin, now the Oscar Wilde Centre of Trinity College Dublin

stops.name: Merrion Square: Speranza receives
stops.date_confidence: the move to 1 Merrion Square North is dated 1855 in the sources with no month or day; both are defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 53.3398, -6.2503 falls inside the square's garden rather than on the north terrace. Wikipedia's Merrion Square centroid is 53.33972, -6.24917 and the Osborne memorial in the park's north-west corner, directly opposite No. 1, is 53.3408, -6.25056; No. 1 stands across the road from that.
stops.campa: The family moves three streets to a Georgian terrace on the north side of Merrion Square, and the first-floor drawing room becomes the best-known salon in Dublin. Speranza receives on Saturday afternoons with the curtains drawn against the daylight, talking sedition and Greek to doctors, antiquarians and young men who write. Downstairs Sir William catalogues the megalithic remains of the west of Ireland. The boy listens to both floors. He is an infant when they move in, and the house is his until he is sent north to school at nine.
stops.quote: Disobedience, in the eyes of anyone who has read history, is man's original virtue.
stops.quote_source: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), text at marxists.org. Written thirty-six years after the move to Merrion Square, and attached here to the room in which he first heard the argument made.
suggested_refs: 1 Merrion Square North, Dublin, and Jane Wilde's Saturday afternoons

stops.name: Portora Royal School, Enniskillen: the classics prizes
stops.date_confidence: the school years are given as 1864 to 1871 without a term date; month and day are defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 54.3467, -7.6389 is Enniskillen town centre (Wikipedia's Enniskillen point is 54.34472, -7.63889), while Portora Royal School's own Wikipedia coordinate is 54.351, -7.655, about 1.15 km north-west on the ridge above Lower Lough Erne.
stops.campa: At nine he is sent north to Portora, on the ridge above Lower Lough Erne, and boards there for seven years. He is useless at games and formidable at Greek, reading ahead of whatever the masters set and carrying off the classics prizes at the end. Boys remember him telling stories after lights out and imitating the staff to their faces. He leaves in 1871 with a Royal School scholarship to Trinity College Dublin and his name cut into the honours board in the hall.
suggested_refs: Portora Royal School, Enniskillen, and its classics honours boards

stops.name: Moytura House, Cong: the summers on Lough Corrib
stops.date_confidence: the summers at Moytura run from the mid 1860s into the early 1870s; the year here orders the segment and is not a documented arrival. Coordinates are approximate, taken from mayo-ireland.ie and the Buildings of Ireland listing; the house is a private dwelling and is not visible from the lane.
stops.campa: Sir William builds a plain house at Gortacurra above Lough Corrib, in the Mayo country where he digs raths and copies inscriptions, and the family summers there through Oscar's boyhood. The father takes his sons out among the cairns and writes a book on the lough and its antiquities. From the cottages around it he collects the stories his wife will later publish under her own name as Irish folklore, along with the charms and the cures and the accounts of what the dead are still owed by the living.
suggested_refs: Moytura House, Gortacurra, near Cong, County Mayo, and Sir William Wilde's Lough Corrib (1867)
sources: Buildings of Ireland listing, Moytura House

stops.name: Edgeworthstown: Isola dies at nine
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The place is corrected away from Dublin: the standard biographical account, followed by Ellmann, puts Isola's death at Edgeworthstown, County Longford, at the house of her uncle the rector, where she had been sent to recuperate. Wikipedia confirms only that she died at nine of a febrile illness, without date or place. The day, 23 February 1867, is standard in the biographies but could not be re-confirmed from a fetchable source in this pass, and the coordinate for Edgeworthstown is a village-centre value, not the rectory.
stops.campa: His sister Isola, two years younger, is sent to their uncle the rector at Edgeworthstown, in County Longford, to recover from a fever. She dies there, nine years old. Oscar is twelve. Twelve years later he prints a short elegy for her in his first collection, six stanzas of plain metre with no aesthetic ornament anywhere in them, written flat against everything he will afterwards argue about art. It is the one poem in that book no reviewer accuses him of having borrowed from somebody else. He never writes about her again.
suggested_refs: Requiescat, in Poems (1881); the rectory at Edgeworthstown, County Longford
sources: Richard Ellmann, Oscar Wilde (1987), as relayed by the research pool

stops.name: Trinity College Dublin: the Berkeley Gold Medal
stops.date_confidence: the scholarship and matriculation are dated 1871 without a day; the month is set to the start of the academic year and the day defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 53.3438, -6.2546 sits about 215 metres east-south-east of Front Square, on the far side of the campus. Wikipedia's Trinity College Dublin point is 53.3444, -6.2577.
stops.campa: He enters Trinity at seventeen and falls under John Pentland Mahaffy, the classicist who will later take him through Greece, and under R. Y. Tyrrell. He wins the Berkeley Gold Medal in Greek, the highest classical honour the college awards, and reads a paper of his own called Aesthetic Morality to the University Philosophical Society. Three years is all he takes from Dublin. In 1874 he sits for a demyship at Magdalen College, Oxford, worth about ninety-five pounds a year, and gets it.
suggested_refs: The Berkeley Gold Medal in Greek, Trinity College Dublin, 1874

segments.name: Oxford: Ruskin's Road and the Double First

stops.name: Magdalen College, Oxford: the demyship
stops.date_confidence: the demyship and residence are attested for 1874 to 1878 (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde); the month is set to the start of Michaelmas term and the day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He comes up to Magdalen in October 1874 on a demyship worth ninety-five pounds a year and stays four years, reading Literae Humaniores in a college that expects gentlemen and gets a performance instead. He furnishes his rooms with blue china, sits under Walter Pater and John Ruskin in the same terms, and builds a manner the undergraduate papers begin quoting back at him. In 1878 he takes a double first, the highest result the school awards, in Classical Moderations and in Greats.
stops.quote: ...the two great turning-points in my life were when my father sent me to Oxford, and when society sent me to prison.
stops.quote_source: De Profundis, written at Reading Gaol 1897, Project Gutenberg e-text no. 921. Quoted with a leading ellipsis: in the manuscript the words are a subordinate clause of a longer sentence beginning 'I want to get to the point when I shall be able to say quite simply, and without affectation...'
suggested_refs: Magdalen College, Oxford, and the demyship registers for 1874

stops.name: North Hinksey: Ruskin's road-menders
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved here. Wikipedia (North Hinksey) dates the road-building project to 1874 and names Wilde in the gang; but Wilde only came up in October 1874, and the research pool's own entry gave 1875 to 1876, so the two datings cannot both be right and the year here is a placeholder inside the overlap. The village is corrected: the diggings were at North Hinksey (Ferry Hinksey), 51.749, -1.292, not at South Hinksey, 51.728, -1.268, which the pool gave and which lies 2.7 km away across the flood meadow.
stops.campa: John Ruskin has persuaded a gang of undergraduates that the road through the marshy meadow at Ferry Hinksey ought to be mended by hand, by them, as an argument in stone about labour and beauty. Wilde takes a barrow. So do Alfred Milner, Hardwicke Rawnsley, Arnold Toynbee and William Gershom Collingwood. Ruskin breakfasts them afterwards and lectures over the plates on the dignity of the work. Wilde takes from him what Pater never offers, that beauty arrives with an obligation attached, and will boast for years that he was given the master's own wheelbarrow. The road is never finished.
suggested_refs: The Ferry Hinksey road diggings and Ruskin's Oxford drawing school

stops.name: Merrion Square: Sir William Wilde dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde, corroborated against the Wilde family chronology). The state of the estate and Lady Wilde's removal to London are standard biography rather than items in the verified research pool, and are given here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Sir William Wilde dies at Merrion Square in the spring of Oscar's second year at Oxford. The knighted surgeon, the medical census, the antiquarian papers and the Mayo house all go into an estate that cannot cover what is owed against it. Within a few years Lady Wilde gives up the square, moves to London, and reopens a smaller version of her afternoons in rooms she cannot afford. Oscar is twenty-one, halfway through a double first, and now the head of nothing in particular. He goes back for the Trinity term.
suggested_refs: Sir William Wilde's Irish medical census and his Lough Corrib antiquarian papers

stops.name: Rome: the audience with Pius IX
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The papal audience of 1877 is well attested in the scholarship, including the Dictionary of Irish Biography, but was not independently re-fetched in this pass; the month and day are placeholders and only the year is claimed.
stops.campa: Travelling in Italy in his third year, Wilde is received in audience by Pius IX, in the second to last year of the longest pontificate in the history of the Church. He has been circling Rome since he came up, drawn to it and frightened of it in the same movement; friends expect him to convert at any week's notice and he keeps not doing it. He writes sonnets about the city and the Pope and prints them. The conversion is postponed twenty-three years, to a bed in a Paris hotel, with a priest bending over it and Wilde past speech.
suggested_refs: Wilde's Roman sonnets of 1877; Dictionary of Irish Biography, Oscar Wilde
sources: Dictionary of Irish Biography, as relayed by the research pool

stops.name: Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford: Ravenna
stops.date_confidence: the Newdigate Prize and the double first are attested for 1878 (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde). The recitation date of 26 June and the Sheldonian venue follow the customary form of the prize-poem ceremony and were not independently re-fetched, so the day is reconstruction rather than a documented record.
stops.campa: The Newdigate is the university's prize for English verse and in 1878 it goes to a poem on Ravenna, a city Wilde had seen the year before on the way back from Greece with Mahaffy. He recites it under Wren's painted ceiling to a full house. Magdalen prints it. He is twenty-three, holds a double first and a prize poem, speaks in an Oxford accent laid over a Dublin one, and has no profession. He tells friends he means to be famous, and does not yet say at what.
suggested_refs: Ravenna (Oxford, 1878), the Newdigate prize poem

stops.name: Chickering Hall, New York: the English Renaissance of Art
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Wikipedia (Chickering Hall, New York City) confirms the 9 January 1882 lecture, and oscarwildeinamerica.org confirms the total of 141 lectures. Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 40.7364, -73.9903, which is about 310 metres south of the hall and shares its longitude with the Union Square Theatre entry, apparently a copied value. Chickering Hall stood at 130 Fifth Avenue at the north-west corner of Eighteenth Street, 40.73889, -73.99194.
stops.campa: He lands from the Arizona at the beginning of January for a lecture tour of the United States and Canada. A week later he stands at Chickering Hall, on Fifth Avenue at Eighteenth Street, in knee breeches, and delivers The English Renaissance of Art to a paying house. The sentence everybody remembers from the tour, the one spoken at the customs desk, is not printed anywhere until ten years after he is dead. A hundred and forty-one lectures follow over eleven months, from the eastern cities out to Salt Lake City and San Francisco and back.
stops.quote: I have nothing to declare except my genius.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Wilde at New York customs, January 1882, and tagged [R]: no contemporary newspaper or customs record attests it. Quote Investigator traces the earliest appearance to 1910, in The Oscar Wilde Calendar compiled by Stuart Mason (Christopher Sclater Millard), and then to Arthur Ransome (1912) and Walter Jerrold (1912); Robert Ross may have supplied the line to Millard and Ransome both.
suggested_refs: Chickering Hall, 130 Fifth Avenue, New York; oscarwildeinamerica.org, the 1882 lecture itinerary
sources: Quote Investigator, 'Nothing to declare except my genius'

stops.name: Camden, New Jersey: Walt Whitman at home
stops.date_confidence: the visit is attested; the address is corrected and the correction contradicts two sources. Wikipedia (Walt Whitman) states that Whitman lived from 1873 at his brother George's house, 431 Stevens Street, Camden, and bought the Mickle Street house only in 1884, and it places the Wilde visit at Stevens Street explicitly. Wikipedia's own Walt Whitman House article nonetheless repeats the claim that Wilde visited at Mickle Street, which is how the error reached the research pool. The Stevens Street coordinate here is approximate; the house is demolished.
stops.campa: He asks to be taken to Whitman and he is: across the Delaware to Camden, to the house on Stevens Street where the poet is living with his brother, sixty-two years old and half paralysed. They talk, and they drink together, for most of an afternoon. Wilde has grown up on Leaves of Grass. Everything past the visit itself, the elderberry wine, the kiss, the erotics that later readers have wanted in that room, comes out of remarks made years afterwards rather than from anything either man wrote down at the time.
suggested_refs: 431 Stevens Street, Camden, the George Whitman house, demolished; Library of Congress Whitman papers
sources: Library of Congress, Walt Whitman collection

stops.name: Leadville, Colorado: the bottom of the Matchless shaft
stops.date_confidence: the Leadville visit is dated to April 1882 in the Colorado Springs Gazette and Irish America accounts; the day is not fixed in the reachable sources and is defaulted to 01. The subject of the lecture, the Florentine goldsmiths and Benvenuto Cellini, is standard in the accounts of the evening but is not itself in the verified research pool.
stops.campa: Two miles above sea level, in a silver town with a reputation for shooting at lecturers, he reads to the miners on the ethics of art and the Florentine goldsmiths and finds them the best-dressed and most courteous audience of the whole tour. They set whiskey out in rounds afterwards, and the Irishman in the velvet coat outlasts them. Then Horace Tabor has him lowered in a bucket down the Matchless shaft at midnight, where he opens a new lode with a silver drill. The miners name it The Oscar.
suggested_refs: The Matchless Mine, Fryer Hill, Leadville, and the lode named The Oscar
sources: Colorado Springs Gazette, Wilde in Leadville

stops.name: Paris: Victor Hugo receives him
stops.date_confidence: the Paris residence and the meeting with Hugo are attested for 1883 (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde) without a month or day; the month here orders the segment and the day is defaulted to 01. The exact lodging is not confirmed and the canonical central Paris pin, 48.8566 / 2.3522, in wide use across the corpus, is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: With American money he takes rooms in Paris and sets out to be received. He restyles himself from the head down, cuts his hair after a bust of Nero, drops the knee breeches, and calls on the writers. Victor Hugo receives him. The old man is eighty-one, two years from his death, the last standing monument of French Romanticism, and Wilde presents himself as the next thing coming. He writes The Duchess of Padua here, in blank verse, for an American actress. Paris will take him back seventeen years later with nothing in his pockets at all.
suggested_refs: The Duchess of Padua (1883), written in Paris for Mary Anderson

stops.name: Union Square Theatre, New York: Vera closes in a week
stops.date_confidence: the premiere and rapid closure are dated to August 1883 in the standard theatrical record; the day is not fixed in the reachable sources and is defaulted to 01. The venue is given as the Union Square Theatre in the research pool with the note that the theatre name is approximate and was not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: He crosses back to New York in August for the production of Vera, his play about Russian nihilists, with Marie Prescott in the title part. The notices are merciless and the run closes inside a week. He has now written two plays and neither has held a stage for a fortnight. For the next two years he lectures through provincial England on dress, on house decoration, on his impressions of America, filling small halls in towns whose inhabitants have read about him in the comic papers and want to see whether he is real.
suggested_refs: Vera; or, The Nihilists (New York, 1883), with Marie Prescott
sources: Standard theatrical record of the Vera premiere, as relayed by the research pool

stops.name: St James's, Paddington: marrying Constance Lloyd
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and doubly confirmed (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde, and Wikipedia, Constance Lloyd); the research pool tagged this [R], which is too weak. Coordinate corrected by about 210 metres: Wikipedia's St James's Church, Paddington, in Sussex Gardens, is 51.513, -0.1765, and the pool's 51.5142, -0.1741 lies north-east of it.
stops.campa: Constance Lloyd is twenty-five, the daughter of an Irish barrister, well read and shy in company. They marry at St James's in Sussex Gardens on the twenty-ninth of May and honeymoon in Paris. Cyril is born the following June, Vyvyan seventeen months after that. For ten years Wilde is a married man in Chelsea with two small sons, and the stories he makes up for them at bedtime go into print as The Happy Prince and Other Tales, five of them, in 1888.
suggested_refs: St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, Paddington; The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888)

stops.name: Tite Street, Chelsea: the house of white and yellow
stops.date_confidence: the family is settled at 16 Tite Street, now No. 34, from January 1885 to 1895 (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde; Historic England listing). Coordinate corrected and reconciled: the research pool carried three separate Tite Street values, 51.4875 / -0.1653 twice and 51.4875 / -0.1699 once, all of them between 420 and 710 metres north-west of the street. Wikipedia's Tite Street point is 51.48535, -0.16029, and that single value is used for every Tite Street stop in this file. Edward Godwin's decorative scheme is standard biography rather than an item in the verified pool.
stops.campa: Edward Godwin does over the house at number sixteen: white and yellow rooms, a dining room in white and grey, a ceiling of Japanese feathers, and almost no pattern anywhere in a decade that cannot get enough of pattern. Constance runs it on two incomes and it is always short. Wilde writes upstairs. This is the address on the manuscripts of Dorian Gray and of Earnest, and the address the reporters print in April 1895, when the bailiffs put the manuscripts and the children's toys under the hammer together to satisfy the costs of a case he brought himself.
suggested_refs: 16 (now 34) Tite Street, Chelsea; the auction of the household contents, April 1895

stops.name: London: The Woman's World and the decay of lying
stops.date_confidence: the editorship runs 1887 to 1889 and 'The Decay of Lying' appeared in the Nineteenth Century in January 1889; the stop is dated to the start of the editorship with month and day defaulted to 01. The Cassell's office in La Belle Sauvage Yard is not given a coordinate in the pool, so the canonical central London pin, 51.5074 / -0.1278, is used. The acquaintance with W. B. Yeats is reconstruction: the research dossier lists Yeats among Wilde's overlapping literary networks without particulars, and Yeats's own journey file carries no mention of Wilde.
stops.campa: Cassell's hires him to edit a fashion monthly called The Lady's World. Within a year he has renamed it The Woman's World and turned it into a review that prints suffrage, university education for women, and his own mother. He is bored of the office within two years and lets the contract lapse. The Irish writing colony in London passes through his rooms in these years, W. B. Yeats among them. At the same desk he writes a dialogue arguing that art owes nothing whatever to nature, and that the imitation runs the other way round.
stops.quote: Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life. This results not merely from Life's imitative instinct, but from the fact that the self-conscious aim of Life is to find expression.
stops.quote_source: The Decay of Lying: An Observation, Nineteenth Century, January 1889; revised for Intentions (1891). Project Gutenberg e-text of Intentions.
suggested_refs: The Woman's World, 1887-1889, Cassell and Company; Intentions (1891)
sources: The Decay of Lying (1891), Project Gutenberg e-text

stops.name: Tite Street: Dorian Gray and the year of prose
stops.date_confidence: Dorian Gray appeared in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in July 1890, cut before printing, and in the expanded twenty-chapter book edition from Ward, Lock in April 1891; the stop is dated to the magazine appearance with the day defaulted to 01. Intentions, Lord Arthur Savile's Crime and Other Stories, A House of Pomegranates and 'The Soul of Man under Socialism' all follow in 1891.
stops.campa: Dorian Gray appears first in Lippincott's in July, cut before printing by an editor who thought it indecent, and is attacked in the newspapers as a poisonous book. Wilde answers every reviewer in the letters columns, then expands the thing from thirteen chapters to twenty for the book and bolts a preface of aphorisms to the front of it. The following year he publishes Intentions, two volumes of stories, and an essay arguing that private property ought to be abolished so that nobody need be obliged to be charitable about it any longer.
stops.quote: It is immoral to use private property in order to alleviate the horrible evils that result from the institution of private property.
stops.quote_source: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), text at marxists.org
suggested_refs: The Picture of Dorian Gray, Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, July 1890, and the Ward, Lock edition of April 1891
sources: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), marxists.org

segments.name: Douglas, Salome, and the West End

stops.name: Cafe Royal, Regent Street: Lord Alfred Douglas
stops.date_confidence: the introduction, probably through Lionel Johnson, is dated to 1891 without a month or day; the month here orders the segment and the day is defaulted to 01. The relationship becomes intimate in 1892-93. The Cafe Royal habit is widely attested in the biographical literature but was not independently re-fetched in this pass.
stops.campa: Lionel Johnson brings Lord Alfred Douglas to Tite Street in 1891. Douglas is twenty-one, an Oxford undergraduate, third son of the Marquess of Queensberry, beautiful, spoiled and already in difficulties. Within two years Wilde is spending on him faster than the plays can earn: the Savoy, the Cafe Royal, suppers at Kettner's, rooms taken and abandoned. In the Domino Room he holds a table most nights, and talks, by every account of it, better than he writes. Almost none of the talk survives.
stops.quote: Selfishness is not living as one wishes to live, it is asking others to live as one wishes to live.
stops.quote_source: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), text at marxists.org
suggested_refs: The Domino Room of the Cafe Royal, Regent Street
sources: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), marxists.org

stops.name: Paris: Salome written in French
stops.date_confidence: the composition date is corrected. The research pool dated the writing to 1892; Wikipedia dates it to Wilde's Paris visit of October 1891 and elsewhere refers to 'the 1891 French play Salome by Oscar Wilde'. What happened in June 1892 was the halting of the London rehearsals by the Lord Chamberlain's examiner, not the writing. The day is defaulted to 01 and the canonical central Paris pin is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: In Paris in October he writes a one-act tragedy in French, a language he does not command perfectly and chooses for exactly that reason, working on the Salome of the gospels, the moon, and the severed head on the dish. He writes it for Sarah Bernhardt. She takes it, and rehearsals open at the Palace Theatre in London the following June with the sets half built. Then the Lord Chamberlain's examiner refuses a licence, under a rule three hundred years old forbidding biblical characters on the public stage, and the production stops where it is standing.
stops.quote: Art is the most intense mode of Individualism that the world has known.
stops.quote_source: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), text at marxists.org
suggested_refs: Salome, French edition, Paris 1893; Richard Strauss's opera Salome, Dresden, 9 December 1905, staged in fifty other houses within two years

stops.name: St James's Theatre: Lady Windermere's Fan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, Lady Windermere's Fan). Coordinate corrected by about 325 metres: Wikipedia's St James's Theatre point is 51.50603, -0.13758, while the pool's 51.5062, -0.1329 lies east of King Street toward Lower Regent Street. The curtain speech is standard in the accounts of the first night but is not itself in the verified pool.
stops.campa: George Alexander produces the first of the society comedies at the St James's on the twentieth of February and it is the hit of the season. He is thirty-seven, and has found, after two failed tragedies and a decade of lecturing, the exact form his talent fits: a drawing room, three acts, and one thing that must not come out. Wilde comes before the curtain at the end holding a lit cigarette and congratulates the audience on their success, which offends the critics and delights everybody else in the building.
stops.quote: The aim of the liar is simply to charm, to delight, to give pleasure. He is the very basis of civilised society.
stops.quote_source: The Decay of Lying (1891), in Intentions, Project Gutenberg e-text
suggested_refs: The St James's Theatre, King Street, demolished 1957; George Alexander's production books

stops.name: Theatre Royal Haymarket: two more, and Queensberry starts following
stops.date_confidence: both premieres are attested to the day: A Woman of No Importance, 19 April 1893, produced by Herbert Beerbohm Tree, and An Ideal Husband, 3 January 1895. The pool credited Tree with both; Tree was in America in January 1895 and the second production was managed by Lewis Waller, so the credit is corrected. Coordinate corrected by about 215 metres: Wikipedia's Theatre Royal Haymarket is 51.5086, -0.1314, against the pool's 51.509, -0.1345.
stops.campa: Herbert Beerbohm Tree produces A Woman of No Importance at the Haymarket in April 1893 and plays Lord Illingworth himself. Twenty-one months later, on the third of January 1895, An Ideal Husband opens on the same stage under Lewis Waller, Tree being away in America. That second play turns on a public man with one buried transaction behind him, on blackmail, and on a wife who has to decide whether she can go on loving him now that she knows what he did. Wilde writes it in the year Queensberry begins following him from restaurant to restaurant.
suggested_refs: Theatre Royal Haymarket; An Ideal Husband, first performed 3 January 1895
sources: Wikipedia, A Woman of No Importance

stops.name: St James's Theatre: The Importance of Being Earnest
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde), with An Ideal Husband still running at the Haymarket, so that Wilde had two plays in the West End at once. The snow and Queensberry's bouquet of vegetables are standard in the accounts of the first night and are not themselves items in the verified pool.
stops.campa: The fourteenth of February, snow lying in King Street, Alexander at the St James's, and Wilde with two plays running in the West End at the same hour. Earnest is the best-built farce in the language and the least sincere thing he ever wrote: three acts, two invented invalids, everybody lying about a name. Queensberry arrives at the theatre carrying a bouquet of vegetables and is turned away at the door by police the management has arranged for. It is the last first night of Wilde's life. Four days later the card is left at the Albemarle.
suggested_refs: The Importance of Being Earnest, St James's Theatre, 14 February 1895

segments.name: The Old Bailey and Reading Gaol

stops.name: Old Bailey: the libel prosecution collapses
stops.date_confidence: the card was left at the Albemarle Club on 18 February 1895; the libel trial ran 3 to 5 April 1895 and the acquittal came on the fifth (famous-trials.com; The London Archives, 'The Three Trials of Oscar Wilde'). Coordinate corrected by about 670 metres: Wikipedia's Old Bailey point is 51.51583, -0.10181, while the pool's longitude of -0.0922 puts the court east of St Paul's near Moorgate.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of February Queensberry leaves a card at the Albemarle Club, addressed to Oscar Wilde posing as a somdomite, the word misspelled in his own hand. Wilde, pushed by Douglas and against the advice of nearly everyone else, prosecutes him for criminal libel. Edward Carson, who was at Trinity with him, appears for the defence and turns the case by producing the young men themselves: grooms, out-of-work clerks, a valet. On the third day Wilde's counsel withdraws. The jury acquits Queensberry and finds his plea of justification proven, which puts Wilde's own conduct on the record as a finding of fact.
suggested_refs: The Queensberry card, Albemarle Club, 18 February 1895; Merlin Holland, The Real Trial of Oscar Wilde (2003)
sources: The London Archives, 'The Three Trials of Oscar Wilde'
famous-trials.com, The Trials of Oscar Wilde

stops.name: Cadogan Hotel, Sloane Street: the arrest
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict and the conflict is not resolved here. famous-trials.com puts the arrest on the evening of 5 April 1895, the same day the libel prosecution collapsed, with the warrant issued at 5 p.m.; Wikipedia states flatly that 'On 6 April 1895, Wilde was arrested for gross indecency'. The reconciliation standard in the biographies, and the one used here, is arrest at the Cadogan on the evening of the fifth, a night at Bow Street, and the formal charge before the magistrate on the sixth. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 51.4928, -0.159 is at the Sloane Square end of the street, while the Cadogan stood at 75 Sloane Street near Pont Street, about 430 metres north; Wikipedia has no coordinate for it, so this value is approximate. The britishnewspaperarchive.com blog cited in the pool returned HTTP 403 and could not be read.
stops.campa: He does not take the boat train. He sits at the Cadogan through the afternoon with Robert Ross while his friends tell him to cross to France and he answers that the last train has gone, which is not yet true. The warrant is signed at five o'clock, by which hour it is. Two officers come up the stairs in the evening. He is taken to Bow Street, held overnight, and charged in the morning under section eleven of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, a clause a journalist named Labouchere had attached to a different bill ten years earlier.
suggested_refs: Section 11 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885, the Labouchere Amendment
sources: famous-trials.com, The Trials of Oscar Wilde

stops.name: Old Bailey: the love that dare not speak its name
stops.date_confidence: the first criminal trial of Wilde and Alfred Taylor opened on 26 April 1895 before Justice Arthur Charles and the jury failed to agree on 1 May; the cross-examination containing this answer took place on 30 April. The pool assigned the testimony to the second criminal trial, which is wrong: C. F. Gill prosecuted the first trial, while the second, 20 to 25 May, was prosecuted by Solicitor-General Frank Lockwood.
stops.campa: He is tried with Alfred Taylor, who kept the rooms where the introductions were made. C. F. Gill leads for the Crown, reads out a poem of Douglas's that ends on the love that dare not speak its name, and asks the defendant what the phrase means. Wilde answers standing, at length, on David and Jonathan, on Plato, on the sonnets of Michelangelo and of Shakespeare. The public gallery breaks into applause and the judge threatens to clear the court. The jury cannot agree on most of the counts. He is bailed on the seventh of May, and again refuses to leave the country.
stops.quote: The love that dare not speak its name in this century is such a great affection of an elder for a younger man as there was between David and Jonathan, such as Plato made the very basis of his philosophy, and such as you find in the sonnets of Michelangelo and Shakespeare. It is that deep, spiritual affection that is as pure as it is perfect... It is in this century misunderstood, so much misunderstood that it may be described as the Love that dare not speak its name, and on account of it I am placed where I am now. It is beautiful, it is fine, it is the noblest form of affection.
stops.quote_source: Testimony at Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, first criminal trial, Old Bailey, 30 April 1895, under cross-examination by C. F. Gill. Verified verbatim against the transcript at famous-trials.com/wilde/342-wildetestimony; the ellipsis stands for 'It dictates and pervades great works of art like those of Shakespeare and Michelangelo, and those two letters of mine, such as they are.'
suggested_refs: The Wilde testimony transcript, famous-trials.com/wilde
sources: The London Archives, 'The Three Trials of Oscar Wilde'

stops.name: Old Bailey: two years with hard labour
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the retrial opened 20 May 1895 and Justice Alfred Wills passed the maximum sentence on 25 May (History.com, 'Oscar Wilde is sent to prison for indecency'; famous-trials.com). The judge's remark that the sentence is totally inadequate for a case such as this is widely quoted from the trial reports and was not separately re-fetched here.
stops.campa: The retrial opens on the twentieth of May with the Solicitor-General himself prosecuting, which is unusual and is noticed at the time. On the twenty-fifth the jury convicts. Justice Alfred Wills gives him the maximum the statute permits, two years with hard labour, and says from the bench that he regards it as totally inadequate for a case such as this. Somebody in the gallery calls out. Wilde tries to say something and is not permitted to, and is taken down the stairs to the cells.
suggested_refs: Justice Alfred Wills's sentencing remarks, Old Bailey, 25 May 1895
sources: History.com, 'Oscar Wilde is sent to prison for indecency'
famous-trials.com, The Trials of Oscar Wilde

stops.name: Wandsworth: the separate system and the bankruptcy
stops.date_confidence: the Pentonville and Wandsworth periods of 1895 are attested by the Oscar Wilde Society biography chronology without exact transfer dates. The bankruptcy adjudication is dated November 1895 and the discharge did not come until 1906; the day is defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected by about 1.26 km: Wikipedia's HM Prison Wandsworth point is 51.45014, -0.17764, against the pool's 51.4567, -0.1926, which lands on the far side of Wandsworth Common. The British Museum's revocation of his Reading Room ticket on 15 June 1895 belongs to this period.
stops.campa: Pentonville first, then Wandsworth: plank bed, treadmill, oakum picking, one hour of exercise, and silence enforced between prisoners as a matter of settled policy. He loses weight quickly, sleeps badly, and is watched by the warders for the signs of breaking. In June the British Museum strikes his Reading Room ticket off the register. In November, with Queensberry's costs taxed against him, he is adjudged bankrupt, and the contents of Tite Street have already gone under the hammer to strangers, manuscripts and children's toys together. The discharge does not come until 1906.
stops.quote: The true perfection of man lies, not in what man has, but in what man is.
stops.quote_source: The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1891), text at marxists.org
suggested_refs: The British Museum Reading Room ticket, revoked 15 June 1895; the British Library reinstated a pass in Wilde's name in October 2025 and gave the card to Merlin Holland
sources: British Library press release, 'British Library symbolically reinstates Oscar Wilde's Reader Pass'

stops.name: Reading Gaol: prisoner C.3.3.
stops.date_confidence: the month is secure and the day is contested: the sources give the transfer to Reading as either 13 or 23 November 1895 and the conflict is not resolved here; the earlier of the two is used. Coordinate corrected by about 700 metres: Wikipedia's HM Prison Reading point is 51.45639, -0.96389, against the pool's -0.9739. The hanging of Charles Thomas Wooldridge at Reading in July 1896 is standard biography; the verified pool records only that the Ballad is organised around his execution.
stops.campa: He is moved to Reading in November and entered on the roll as C.3.3.: block C, third landing, cell three. For two years he is given the number in place of the name. He collapses in the chapel and splits his right ear open on the stone, an injury that never fully closes and that will be waiting for him in a Paris hotel room five years later. In the summer of 1896 a trooper of the Royal Horse Guards is hanged in the yard for cutting his wife's throat, and Wilde, in the exercise ring, has watched the man take his hour with the rest of them.
stops.quote: To shut up a child in a dimly lit cell, for twenty-three hours out of the twenty-four, is an example of the cruelty of stupidity.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Daily Chronicle on prison life, text via Wikisource, 'Two Letters to the Daily Chronicle on Prison Life'
suggested_refs: HM Prison Reading, cell C.3.3.; the execution of Charles Thomas Wooldridge, July 1896
sources: Wikisource, Two Letters to the Daily Chronicle on Prison Life

stops.name: Reading Gaol: the letter to Douglas
stops.date_confidence: the letter was written in the first months of 1897; no start date is recorded and month and day are defaulted to 01. Roughly 50,000 words. Ross published an abridgement in 1905 under a title Wilde never used; a fuller 1949 edition by Vyvyan Holland was still full of transcription errors, and the first accurate complete text appeared only in Rupert Hart-Davis's 1962 edition of the letters, taken from the manuscript held under a fifty-year access restriction Ross himself imposed.
stops.campa: In the last months of the sentence a new governor allows him pen and paper, one sheet at a time, collected again each evening. He writes eighty foolscap pages to Douglas: an account of the friendship, a bill of particulars, and then something else, a reckoning with sorrow as the one condition that cannot be posed. He is not permitted to send it. He carries it out of the gate with him. Ross prints a third of it in 1905 under a title Wilde never used, and no accurate complete text exists until 1962.
stops.quote: Suffering is one very long moment. We cannot divide it by seasons.
stops.quote_source: De Profundis, written 1897, first published in abridged form 1905 by Robert Ross; text via Project Gutenberg e-text
suggested_refs: The De Profundis manuscript, British Library, formerly under a fifty-year restriction; Hart-Davis, Letters of Oscar Wilde (1962)

stops.name: Pentonville: out on the morning of the nineteenth
stops.date_confidence: the release date and the mechanism are both corrected. Wikipedia states 'Wilde was released from prison on 19 May 1897'; he was moved from Reading to Pentonville on the evening of 18 May and released from Pentonville the following morning, so he was not released from Reading Gaol at all, and he crossed to France the same night rather than the next day. Wikipedia's own summary line, 'incarcerated from 25 May 1895 to 18 May 1897', is internally inconsistent with its explicit release sentence; the 19 May date is the one used here.
stops.campa: On the evening of the eighteenth he is taken from Reading to Pentonville in a closed carriage, and on the morning of the nineteenth he walks out of the gate in clothes that no longer fit him, having served every day of the two years without remission. Friends are waiting for him outside. He is forty-two, bankrupt, and has three and a half years left to live, in which he will publish one poem. He crosses to France that same night and does not set foot in England or in Ireland again.
suggested_refs: HM Prison Pentonville, the release of 19 May 1897

stops.name: Dieppe: the name he takes off the boat
stops.date_confidence: he sailed the night of 19 May and reached Dieppe on the morning of the twentieth (Oscar Wilde Society biography chronology). The etymology of Sebastian Melmoth, fusing the martyr with the wanderer of Charles Maturin's novel, is standard in the biographies but was not verified in this pass against a primary document such as a signed hotel register, and is tagged [R].
stops.campa: Robert Ross and Reginald Turner are on the quay at dawn. Wilde comes off the boat carrying a large sealed envelope, talking, apparently in high spirits, and hands over the prison manuscript. Within the week he has taken a new name: Sebastian for the martyr full of arrows, Melmoth out of Melmoth the Wanderer, the novel his great-uncle Charles Maturin wrote about a man who can neither die nor come home. Dieppe is full of English visitors on holiday, and a number of them cross the street rather than pass him. He moves along the coast.
suggested_refs: Charles Maturin, Melmoth the Wanderer (1820)

stops.name: Berneval-le-Grand: the Ballad begun
stops.date_confidence: the Chalet Bourgeat tenancy runs through the summer and autumn of 1897; the month here orders the segment and the day is defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected by about 2.6 km: Wikipedia's Berneval-le-Grand point is 49.9589, 1.1889, against the pool's 49.9411, 1.165. Wikipedia (The Ballad of Reading Gaol) says the poem was begun at Berneval-le-Grand and completed at Naples. The jubilee party for the village children is standard biography, not an item in the verified pool.
stops.campa: He rents the Chalet Bourgeat at Berneval, ten miles along the coast from Dieppe, and for one summer lives well. He gives the village children a party for the Queen's jubilee. He swims. He writes to the London newspapers about prison food and about children held in gaol, and he begins the poem about the trooper hanged at Reading. It is the last sustained writing of his life. He is waiting on Constance to let him see his sons, and on Douglas, and only one of the two answers him.
suggested_refs: Chalet Bourgeat, Berneval-le-Grand, Normandy
sources: Wikipedia, The Ballad of Reading Gaol
LA Weekly, 'A Letter From Oscar Wilde'

stops.name: Posillipo, Naples: the reunion and the end of it
stops.date_confidence: the month of the Rouen reunion is corrected: the pool gave September 1897, but Wikipedia states that Wilde and Douglas 'were reunited in August 1897 at Rouen'. The Naples months follow from the autumn and the separation comes by December; the day is defaulted to 01. The exact villa address on the Posillipo headland was not confirmed and the coordinate is the district only.
stops.campa: He meets Douglas at Rouen in August, on the platform, in front of everyone, and the two go south to a house on the Posillipo headland above the bay. Constance stops his allowance. The Queensberrys threaten to stop Douglas's. Here he finishes The Ballad of Reading Gaol, the only thing he completes in exile, and here the reunion runs out in money, quarrels, and pressure from both families, so that by December they have parted for good. He has been at liberty seven months and has spent every arrangement that was made for him.
suggested_refs: The villa at Posillipo, Naples, autumn 1897
sources: Wikipedia, The Ballad of Reading Gaol

stops.name: Paris: C.3.3. in print, and the letter on prison reform
stops.date_confidence: Leonard Smithers published The Ballad of Reading Gaol in London on 13 February 1898 under the byline C.3.3.; Wilde himself was in Paris and the stop sits at the canonical central Paris pin accordingly. The second Daily Chronicle letter, 'Prison Reform', is dated 23 March 1898 and was published on the twenty-fourth; the pool dated the quotation '1897/1898', which is corrected to 1898. Constance Wilde died at Genoa on 7 April 1898 after gynaecological surgery; Wilde was not present, and no visit by him to the grave is recorded in the verified pool.
stops.campa: Smithers publishes the poem in February under the name C.3.3. rather than under Wilde's, and it sells, edition after edition, to people who do not always know whose it is. Wilde watches this from cafe tables, living on remittances and on whatever he can get from acquaintances passing through Paris. In March he writes to the Daily Chronicle again, this time on the reform bill before Parliament, on the warder dismissed for giving a hungry child a biscuit, and on what the system does to the minds inside it. In April, Constance dies at Genoa after an operation, and he learns of it by letter.
stops.quote: The production of insanity is, if not its object, certainly its result.
stops.quote_source: Second letter to the Daily Chronicle, 'Prison Reform', dated 23 March 1898 and published 24 March 1898; Wikisource, De Profundis (Wilde, 1915)/Two Letters to the Daily Chronicle on Prison Life
suggested_refs: The Ballad of Reading Gaol, Leonard Smithers, London, 13 February 1898, by C.3.3., dedicated to C. T. W.
sources: Wikisource, Two Letters to the Daily Chronicle on Prison Life
University College Oxford, 'The Ballad of Reading Gaol'

stops.name: Paris: calling on Alfred Jarry
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is dated to May 1898 in the French Wikipedia article on Alfred Jarry; the day is not given and is defaulted to 01, and no location within Paris is attested, so the canonical Paris pin is inherited byte for byte from Jarry's own file, where the encounter is already staged from the other side.
stops.campa: He calls on the author of Ubu Roi. Jarry is twenty-five, famous for a single riot at the Theatre de l'Oeuvre, and manufactures his own scandal daily as a working method. Wilde is forty-three, was destroyed by a scandal he did not choose, and is cut in the street by Englishmen who used to dine at his table. Both of them live off the same commodity, from opposite ends of it. Wilde has eighteen months left; Jarry has nine years. What the two of them said to each other that spring is recorded nowhere.
suggested_refs: Alfred Jarry, Ubu Roi, Theatre de l'Oeuvre, December 1896

stops.name: Hotel d'Alsace, rue des Beaux-Arts: the room and the operation
stops.date_confidence: the residence at 13 rue des Beaux-Arts runs from 1898 to his death; the ear operation is dated 10 October 1900 in the pool and is tagged [R] there, the chronic right-ear disease having worsened through that year. The proprietor Jean Dupoirier's forbearance over the bill is standard biography and is not itself in the verified pool.
stops.campa: He settles at last into a small hotel in the rue des Beaux-Arts, where the proprietor Jean Dupoirier feeds him and lets the bill run on unpaid. He writes nothing. He drinks absinthe, talks as well as he ever talked to anyone who will sit down opposite him, and borrows. The ear he split open on the chapel floor at Reading has been discharging for years, and on the tenth of October a surgeon operates in the hotel room. He does not recover from it. Through November the headaches worsen and he cannot always hold on to what is being said to him.
stops.quote: The supreme vice is shallowness. Whatever is realised is right.
stops.quote_source: De Profundis, written at Reading Gaol 1897, Project Gutenberg e-text
suggested_refs: The Hotel d'Alsace, 13 rue des Beaux-Arts, Paris, now L'Hotel

stops.name: Hotel d'Alsace: cerebral meningitis
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested to the day, at about two in the afternoon, officially of cerebral meningitis (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde). The conditional baptism by Father Cuthbert Dunne on 29 November is tagged [R]: it is reported by Dunne and by Robert Ross and is not corroborated by a third witness, and the degree of conscious assent is disputed. The wallpaper epigram is legend; Quote Investigator finds no bedside witness recording it as his last words, and it most likely began as an earlier joke about the room and was recast afterwards.
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of November Ross fetches a Passionist priest, Cuthbert Dunne, who baptises him conditionally and administers the last rites. Whether the man in the bed understands and consents is a question Dunne answers one way, Ross a second, and no third witness answers at all. He dies the following afternoon of cerebral meningitis, forty-six years old, with Ross and Turner in the room. The joke about the wallpaper, the one line of his that everybody can still quote, is recorded by nobody who was actually present.
suggested_refs: Father Cuthbert Dunne's account of the deathbed baptism; Quote Investigator on the wallpaper epigram
sources: Quote Investigator, wallpaper study, as relayed by the research pool

stops.name: Cimetiere de Bagneux: the rented grave
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Ellen Crowell (branchcollective.org) confirms that the Bagneux plot was a temporary concession taken for want of funds, with Ross paying. Coordinate corrected by about 1.4 km: Wikipedia's Cimetiere parisien de Bagneux point is 48.806, 2.309, against the pool's 48.7936, 2.3086, which falls south of the cemetery wall.
stops.campa: Ross pays for the funeral and for a temporary concession at Bagneux, in the southern suburbs, because there is no money for anything better. The plot is rented and not bought, which in a Paris cemetery means it will be cleared and reused in its turn unless somebody comes back for it. Ross starts in at once on the copyrights, which are the whole of what a bankrupt author leaves behind him, and works at them for the best part of a decade. Wilde lies at Bagneux nine years.
suggested_refs: Ellen Crowell, 'Oscar Wilde's Tomb: Silence and the Aesthetics of Queer Memorial', branchcollective.org

stops.name: Pere Lachaise, division 89: the transfer
stops.date_confidence: the transfer is dated 1909 without a month or day; both are defaulted to 01. The research pool carries two different coordinates for the tomb, 48.8595 / 2.3936 from the geography lens and 48.8631 / 2.3934 from the afterlife lens, a discrepancy of roughly 400 metres; the geography value is used here and the conflict is not resolved. Ross's ashes were placed in the tomb in 1950.
stops.campa: In 1909 Ross buys a plot at Pere Lachaise and the remains are taken across Paris and reinterred in division 89. Nine years of executorship stand behind the move: the copyrights recovered, the creditors paid, the bankruptcy discharged in 1906, and enough over at the end of it to buy ground that nobody can rent out again. Ross has held the office since the death and will hold it until his own, in 1918. He leaves instructions that his ashes are to be placed in the same tomb, and in 1950 they are.
suggested_refs: Robert Ross as literary executor, 1900-1918; the placing of his ashes in the tomb, 1950

stops.name: Pere Lachaise: the Epstein monument covered and uncovered
stops.date_confidence: the installation year is corrected. Crowell (branchcollective.org) gives a commission announced at a Ritz dinner in December 1908, two thousand pounds from an anonymous donor later revealed as Helen Carew, the sculpture arriving in Paris in August 1912 and being covered and put under guard at once, and the unveiling only in August 1914 after two years of suppression. The pool gave 1912 as the unveiling. The compromise object fixed over the figure is described by Wikipedia as a bronze butterfly-shaped plaque rather than the plaster the pool named. The chiselling off of the genitals is dated 1961. The day here is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Helen Carew gives two thousand pounds anonymously and Jacob Epstein cuts a flying naked messenger out of a twenty-ton block of Hopton Wood stone, wings back, face forward. It arrives in Paris in August 1912 and the authorities cover it with a tarpaulin and post a guard on it, objecting to the genitals. It stands under wraps for two years. In August 1914 a bronze plaque in the shape of a butterfly is fixed over the offending part, the tomb is opened to view, and Epstein refuses to attend the unveiling. In 1961 somebody arrives with a chisel and removes the whole area.
suggested_refs: Jacob Epstein's tomb sculpture, Pere Lachaise, installed 1912 and unveiled August 1914; Wikipedia, Tomb of Oscar Wilde

stops.name: Merrion Square: the figure on the quartz boulder
stops.date_confidence: the unveiling is dated 1997 without a month or day; both are defaulted to 01. Danny Osborne's three-part sculpture was commissioned by the Guinness Ireland Group and unveiled by Merlin Holland (Wikipedia, Oscar Wilde Memorial Sculpture). The coordinate is the memorial's own point in the north-west corner of the square, opposite No. 1. A second memorial, Maggi Hambling's 'A Conversation with Oscar Wilde', was unveiled on Adelaide Street, London, on 30 November 1998, the anniversary of his death; it is not given a stop here because Wilde had no recorded connection to that street.
stops.campa: Danny Osborne lays a figure of Wilde along a quartz boulder in the north-west corner of the square: jade and pink thulite for the smoking jacket, porcelain for the face, granite and stone fetched from three continents for the rest of him. One side of the mouth smiles and the other side does not. He is looking across the road at the windows of the first-floor drawing room where his mother received on Saturday afternoons. Merlin Holland unveils him in 1997, ninety-seven years after Paris. The brewery pays for it.
suggested_refs: Danny Osborne's Oscar Wilde Memorial Sculpture, Merrion Square, Dublin, 1997; Maggi Hambling, 'A Conversation with Oscar Wilde', Adelaide Street, London, 1998
sources: Wikipedia, A Conversation with Oscar Wilde

stops.name: Pere Lachaise: the kisses and the glass
stops.date_confidence: the restoration and the fitting of the glass panels are dated to November 2011, undertaken by the Irish state in partnership with Merlin Holland (branchcollective.org, Crowell). The day is defaulted to 01. The lipstick tradition grew through the middle of the twentieth century; no single starting date is recorded.
stops.campa: Visitors begin leaving lipstick on the stone, first a few, then thousands, until the base and the wings carry a dense overlapping print of mouths. The grease drives into the limestone and every cleaning takes more of the surface away with it. In November 2011 the Irish state pays for a restoration and Merlin Holland, Wilde's grandson, stands by while glass panels are fitted around the tomb. The kisses now land on the glass. The stone underneath is legible again and out of reach.
suggested_refs: The 2011 restoration of the Wilde tomb and its glass enclosure
